newsitem.title: UK: N.Irish Unionist leader blows cold on Dublin links.
newsitem.headline: N.Irish Unionist leader blows cold on Dublin links.

text.p: Protestant leader David Trimble stepped up pressure for quick progress in Northern Irish peace talks on Sunday, but he ruled out any role for Ireland in administering the British province.

"Why should Dublin have any say in Northern Ireland?" he asked in a BBC television interview. "Why should it exercise power outside its boundaries, over people to whom it is not accountable who have not elected it?"

Trimble, who heads the "pro-British" Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) in multi-party talks, said unionist politicians and their nationalist rivals must make headway fast on ending long-running conflict over rule from London and internal political structures.
He warned that hard-won political momentum could soon be frozen by rivalry for its 18 parliamentary seats in the run-up to a British general election early next year.
"If anything is going to be done (in the talks) before the next general election, it must be done in the next couple of months," he told Reuters.

Trimble said that his party would support "a decent relationship" with neighbouring Ireland. But he signalled there would be no deviation from UUP policy that Ireland must abandon a constitutional claim to the territory.

Britain and Ireland, which are agreed that Northern Ireland remain part of Britain while the Protestant majority supports "the union", set up the talks to end 25 years of strife after a guerrilla war that claimed more than 3,200 lives.

The 40 per cent Catholics, a minority of whom support banned IRA guerrillas, aspire to an all-Ireland free of British influence and early moves to recognise their Irish identity in a range of "cross-border structures".

Sinn Fein, the Irish Republican Army's political wing, is barred from the talks because the guerrillas abandoned a 17- month truce in February with bombs in mainland Britain and one at a military base in Germany.

Trimble, in a weekend speech to his party's annual conference, said that participants in the multi-party talks chaired by former U.S. senator George Mitchell, should press ahead and not "mark time" waiting for Sinn Fein.

The IRA, fighting to end British rule, switched its bombing war to Northern Ireland two weeks ago, attacking British army headquarters in Lisburn, south of Belfast. A soldier was killed and 30 other people wounded in its first action in the province for more than two years.
The escalation threw a pall over the struggling talks and threatened to provoke a backlash by banned Protestant "loyalist" guerrillas who have operated a fragile two year truce.
Loyalist sources said it was up to the major parties to demonstrate that talks not guns could offer the rival communities a new future.
In an unexpected move last week as the Loyalist truce hung in the balance, the UUP and the main nationalist Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP) reached rare accord.
Optimism about a new impetus grew when they agreed a talks agenda after four months of Unionist wrangling about the vexed issue guerrilla disarmament and procedural issues.
But the SDLP, which wants strong links with Ireland, sounded a warning on Sunday that the Mitchell talks might still face stiff problems.

SDLP politicians said the attitude of the three main Unionist parties on how and when IRA guerrillas should disarm might continue to upset progress towards negotiations on possible future economic, trade or political structures on the island.
Senior SDLP negotiator Mark Durkan said there were remaining "differences and difficulties" about "arms decommissioning".

"I will judge Mr Trimble's words by what his party does in relation to issues facing us at the moment and the means by which we will get speedily into substantive negotiations," SDLP deputy leader Seamus Mallon told Reuters.
